claim.pdf_says: 9.1.9   Reel and unit (printed page 221, set in the same bold heading style and at the same left margin as the three-component headings 9.1.5, 9.1.6, 9.1.7 on printed page 219, i.e. a sibling of 9.1.8 Access modes - not a child of it)
claim.why_it_matters: The transcription's convention in this chapter renders three-component 9.1.x sections at '##' (9.1.3 through 9.1.8, 9.1.10-9.1.13 are all '##') and four-component 9.1.x.y sections at '###'. 9.1.9 Reel and unit is transcribed at '###', the same depth as its immediate predecessors 9.1.8.2/9.1.8.3/9.1.8.4, so every outline/TOC consumer nests 9.1.9 inside 9.1.8 Access modes. Reel and unit is not part of access modes. This heading-level scheme is inconsistent elsewhere in the same chapter too (9.1 is '###' with 9.1.1/9.1.2 at '####', and 9.1.13.8 is '##' among '###' siblings), so the repair should be a level sweep of chapter 9.1 rather than a one-line edit.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on four independent grounds; nothing from the PDF is missing or altered. 1. NOTHING IS MISSING - the 'kind' is self-refuting. The heading is present in the transcription verbatim, with its full section number, its exact title, and an id anchor: '' / '### 9.1.9 Reel and unit' (page-251.md lines 27-28; ISO_COBOL.md line 11180). The claim's own 'markdown_says' field quotes the heading it calls missing. A 'missing-heading' finding requires absent text; the only thing that differs is the count of '#' characters in the ATX marker. 2. THE ALLEGED PDF SIGNAL DOES NOT EXIST - I looked at the printed glyphs on both pages. The claim's inference is that because 9.1.9 is set in the same bold face and at the same left margin as 9.1.5/9.1.6/9.1.7, the PDF marks it as a three-component sibling of 9.1.8. That inference is invalid, because ISO sets EVERY heading in this clause identically regardless of depth. On printed page 221 (PDF 251) the four-component headings '9.1.8.2 Sequential access mode', '9.1.8.3 Random access mode', '9.1.8.4 Dynamic access mode' and the three-component '9.1.9 Reel and unit' are all the same bold serif, the same point size, at the same left margin, with the same tab gap after the number - I can see no typographic difference of any kind between them. I rendered printed page 219 (PDF 249) to test the claim's own baseline: there, '9.1.7 Organization' (three-component) and '9.1.7.1 General' / '9.1.7.2 Sequential' (four-component) are likewise typographically indistinguishable. The ISO PDF encodes heading depth SOLELY in the dotted section number, and the transcription reproduces that number exactly ('9.1.9'). There is no depth information in the PDF for the markdown to have lost. 3. THE 'CONVENTION' THE TRANSCRIPTION SUPPOSEDLY VIOLATES IS NOT A CONVENTION. The claim asserts a rule of three-component='##' / four-component='###'. The file contradicts it on both sides, adjacent to the cited heading: '## 9.1.8.1 General' (11143), '## 9.1.7.3 Relative' (11118) and '## 9.1.7.4 Indexed' (11129) are four-component sections at '##', and '## 9.1.13.2' (11290) / '## 9.1.13.8' (11457) likewise. Worse, the '##' sections the claim treats as the correct depth for 9.1.9 sit at the SAME level as the chapter itself ('## 9 I-O, objects, and user-defined functions', 11007) and DEEPER-numbered-but-shallower than their own parent clause ('### 9.1 Files', 11010, with '#### 9.1.1'/'#### 9.1.2' beneath it). The same shape recurs in the next clause ('## 9.2 Screens' with '### 9.2.1'-'### 9.2.4' then '## 9.2.5'-'## 9.2.7'). ATX depth in this transcription is simply not correlated with section depth anywhere in the file, so 9.1.9 at '###' is indistinguishable from ambient noise rather than a page-251 defect. 4. NO SPEC CONTENT DIFFERS. Section number, title, and body text on printed page 221 match the transcription word for word, including the body: "The terms 'reel' and 'unit' are synonymous. They are applicable only to files with sequential organization that are associated with a physical file that may be contained on multiple physical devices. Treatment of ...". The printed page breaks mid-sentence after 'Treatment of' and the transcription joins the continuation from the following page - ordinary paragraph reflow across a page break, an explicit rejection criterion, not a discrepancy. This is markdown presentation, not specification content - also an explicit rejection criterion. Nothing about deriving or citing COBOL behavior depends on ATX depth: citations in this project are by section number ('ISO/IEC 1989:2023 section 9.1.9'), and both the number and its '#section-9-1-9' anchor are intact and resolvable. The claim's own remedy ('a level sweep of chapter 9.1 rather than a one-line edit') concedes that this is not a page-251 finding at all; and even that remedy is under-scoped, since the defect covers the chapter and clause headings themselves and repeats file-wide.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. Section 9.1.9 'Reel and unit' is transcribed completely and accurately on page 251 - number, title, anchor, and body text all match the printed page 221 exactly. The ISO PDF conveys heading depth only through the dotted section number, never through type style or left margin: verified that 9.1.8.2/9.1.8.3/9.1.8.4 (four-component) and 9.1.9 (three-component) are typographically identical on printed page 221, as are 9.1.7 and 9.1.7.1/9.1.7.2 on printed page 219. So no depth information was available in the source to lose. Separately - and outside the scope of a page-level reconciliation - the transcription's ATX heading depths are uncorrelated with section depths throughout the whole file, not just at 9.1.9: '## 9' sits at the same level as '## 9.1.3', beneath '### 9.1 Files'; four-component 9.1.7.3, 9.1.7.4, 9.1.8.1, 9.1.13.2 and 9.1.13.8 are at '##'; and clause 9.2 shows the identical pattern. If the owner wants clean machine-readable outlining, that is a single file-wide cosmetic pass deriving each heading's level from its dot count, tracked as a transcription-pipeline task - not a spec-content reconciliation item, and not a defect attributable to page 251.
